warmup.q: A Kotlin adapter implements fun interface Gateway { fun charge(amountMinor: Long): String } and calls a vendor method that throws IOException, with no try/catch. What happens when the vendor throws?
options: It doesn't compile: the IOException must be caught or declared
The IOException travels straight through the port to whoever called charge
The exception is swallowed and charge returns an empty string
warmup.why: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the code compiles and the vendor's IOException reaches your service code through a port that never mentioned it. In Java the same adapter would not compile, because the port's method doesn't declare IOException. Translating vendor errors at the boundary is a habit you need in Kotlin.

sections.h: Adapter: make their API fit your port
sections.html:
An adapter converts the interface of a class you can't change into the interface your code expects. In payments you write them all the time: the issuer gives you a SOAP SDK, a PSP gives you an HTTP client with its own types, and one acquirer still sends fixed-width files. Your payment logic should see none of that. It should see your own port, in your own words:

Java
interface PaymentGateway {
    String charge(long amountMinor, String currency, String token);
}
Kotlin
fun interface PaymentGateway {
    fun charge(amountMinor: Long, currency: String, token: String): String
}

The adapter implements the port and holds the vendor object. All translation happens inside it, in both directions: your types into the vendor's on the way in, the vendor's results and errors into yours on the way out.

Java
record SoapGatewayAdapter(LegacySoapClient soap) implements PaymentGateway {
    public String charge(long amountMinor, String currency, String token) {
        String xml = "<txn amt='" + amountMinor + "' cur='" + currency + "' tok='" + token + "'/>";
        try {
            String resp = soap.submitTxn(xml);
            return resp.substring(resp.indexOf("ref='") + 5, resp.lastIndexOf("'"));   // vendor format ends here
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new GatewayUnavailable("issuer unreachable", e);                       // our exception, not theirs
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class SoapGatewayAdapter(private val soap: LegacySoapClient) : PaymentGateway {
    override fun charge(amountMinor: Long, currency: String, token: String): String {
        val xml = "<txn amt='$amountMinor' cur='$currency' tok='$token'/>"
        try {
            val resp = soap.submitTxn(xml)
            return resp.substringAfter("ref='").substringBefore("'")          // vendor format ends here
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            throw GatewayUnavailable("issuer unreachable", e)                 // our exception, not theirs
        }
    }
}

The most common adapter bug is a leaky one. If IOException, the vendor's response codes or its DTOs show up in your service layer, every caller now depends on the vendor, and switching issuers means changing all of them.

Java's checked exceptions help here, almost by accident. The port doesn't declare IOException, so javac won't let the vendor's exception escape the adapter. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the same leak compiles without a word. In Kotlin, the discipline is yours.

When the port has one method, you don't need a class at all: a lambda or method reference is the adapter, in both languages.

try.title: Let the vendor's exception leak
steps: Run SoapAdapterDemo in either language with the command below. Read the three lines.
In the Java version, delete the try/catch in SoapGatewayAdapter.charge, keeping the two lines inside the try. Predict, then run.
Do the same in the Kotlin version. Predict, then run. Restore both files.

code.title: SoapAdapterDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l04; import java.io.IOException; import java.util.function.BiFunction; /** A legacy SOAP client adapted to our port, plus a lambda adapter for a one-method port. */ public class SoapAdapterDemo { // the port our payment code depends on interface PaymentGateway { String charge(long amountMinor, String currency, String token); } // a vendor client we can't change: XML in, XML out, checked IOException on failure static final class LegacySoapClient { String submitTxn(String xml) throws IOException { if (xml.contains("tok_down")) throw new IOException("SOAP fault: 503 Service Unavailable"); String token = xml.substring(xml.indexOf("tok='") + 5, xml.lastIndexOf("'")); return "<resp code='00' ref='R-" + token.toUpperCase() + "'/>"; } } static final class GatewayUnavailable extends RuntimeException { GatewayUnavailable(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); } } // the adapter: implements our port, holds the vendor client, translates both ways record SoapGatewayAdapter(LegacySoapClient soap) implements PaymentGateway { public String charge(long amountMinor, String currency, String token) { String xml = "<txn amt='" + amountMinor + "' cur='" + currency + "' tok='" + token + "'/>"; try { String resp = soap.submitTxn(xml); return resp.substring(resp.indexOf("ref='") + 5, resp.lastIndexOf("'")); // vendor format ends here } catch (IOException e) { throw new GatewayUnavailable("issuer unreachable", e); // our exception, not theirs } } } // for a one-method port, a lambda is the adapter static PaymentGateway fromFunction(BiFunction<Long, String, String> legacyCharge) { return (amount, currency, token) -> legacyCharge.apply(amount, token); } public static void main(String[] args) { PaymentGateway gateway = new SoapGatewayAdapter(new LegacySoapClient()); System.out.println("charged, ref " + gateway.charge(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42")); try { gateway.charge(1_250, "EUR", "tok_down"); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("caller sees " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } PaymentGateway quick = fromFunction((amount, token) -> "QUICK-" + amount); System.out.println("lambda adapter: " + quick.charge(990, "EUR", "tok_7")); } }

alt.title: SoapAdapterDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l04 import java.io.IOException // A legacy SOAP client adapted to our port, plus a lambda adapter for a one-method port. // the port our payment code depends on fun interface PaymentGateway { fun charge(amountMinor: Long, currency: String, token: String): String } // a vendor client we can't change: XML in, XML out, IOException on failure class LegacySoapClient { @Throws(IOException::class) fun submitTxn(xml: String): String { if ("tok_down" in xml) throw IOException("SOAP fault: 503 Service Unavailable") val token = xml.substringAfter("tok='").substringBefore("'") return "<resp code='00' ref='R-${token.uppercase()}'/>" } } class GatewayUnavailable(message: String, cause: Throwable) : RuntimeException(message, cause) // the adapter: implements our port, holds the vendor client, translates both ways class SoapGatewayAdapter(private val soap: LegacySoapClient) : PaymentGateway { override fun charge(amountMinor: Long, currency: String, token: String): String { val xml = "<txn amt='$amountMinor' cur='$currency' tok='$token'/>" try { val resp = soap.submitTxn(xml) return resp.substringAfter("ref='").substringBefore("'") // vendor format ends here } catch (e: IOException) { throw GatewayUnavailable("issuer unreachable", e) // our exception, not theirs } } } fun main() { val gateway: PaymentGateway = SoapGatewayAdapter(LegacySoapClient()) println("charged, ref " + gateway.charge(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42")) try { gateway.charge(1_250, "EUR", "tok_down") } catch (e: Exception) { println("caller sees ${e.javaClass.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } // for a fun interface, a lambda is the adapter (SAM conversion) val quick = PaymentGateway { amount, _, _ -> "QUICK-$amount" } println("lambda adapter: " + quick.charge(990, "EUR", "tok_7")) }

try.expect: Both versions print charged, ref R-TOK_42, caller sees GatewayUnavailable: issuer unreachable and lambda adapter: QUICK-990. Without the catch, Java refuses to compile: unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown. Kotlin compiles and prints caller sees IOException: SOAP fault: 503 Service Unavailable: the vendor's exception walked through your port.

sections.h: Extension functions are Kotlin's light adapters
sections.html:
Kotlin has a lighter adapter for data: the extension function. The issuer SDK hands you a VendorTxn with fields called amt, ccyNum and respCd, and you want your own Receipt. Write the mapping once, as an extension on the vendor type:

Java
// Java has no extension functions: the same adapter is a static method
static Receipt toReceipt(VendorTxn txn) {
    Currency currency = Currency.getAvailableCurrencies().stream()
            .filter(c -> c.getNumericCode() == Integer.parseInt(txn.ccyNum()))
            .findFirst().orElseThrow();
    return new Receipt(txn.txnRef(),
            new BigDecimal(txn.amt()).movePointRight(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits()).longValueExact(),
            currency.getCurrencyCode(), txn.respCd().equals("00"));
}

List<Receipt> receipts = fromSdk.stream().map(Adapters::toReceipt).toList();
Kotlin
fun VendorTxn.toReceipt(): Receipt {
    val currency = Currency.getAvailableCurrencies().first { it.numericCode == ccyNum.toInt() }
    return Receipt(
        reference = txnRef,
        amountMinor = BigDecimal(amt).movePointRight(currency.defaultFractionDigits).longValueExact(),
        currency = currency.currencyCode,
        approved = respCd == "00",
    )
}

val receipts = fromSdk.map { it.toReceipt() }

An extension function is not part of the class. It compiles to a static method that takes the receiver as its first parameter, which is exactly the Java twin. What changes is how the call reads, txn.toReceipt(), and where the IDE offers it: type txn. and it appears next to the vendor's own methods.

Two rules keep these adapters honest. Keep them in your adapter package, next to the code that calls the SDK, and not in a shared utils file: they are part of the translation layer. And use them for data, not for behavior. An extension can't hold state, can't implement your port, and can't be replaced in a test. When you need something your service depends on, write a port and a class.

The other light adapter in Kotlin is the fun interface. PaymentGateway { amount, _, _ -> legacy.pay(amount) } builds an adapter from a lambda, the same way a Java lambda implements a functional interface.

steps: Read ExtensionAdapters.kt (or its Java twin). Predict the three receipts, and look hard at the yen one.

sections.h: Facade: one call for a job with several steps
sections.html:
A facade gives callers one simple entry point to a subsystem. Checkout is the classic case: reserve stock, charge the card, post to the ledger, send a receipt. If every caller (the REST resource, the Kafka consumer for marketplace orders, the admin tool) makes those calls itself, each gets the order and the failure handling slightly different. Put the sequence in one class:

Java
record CheckoutFacade(Inventory inventory, Payments payments, Notifier notifier) {
    String checkout(String sku, long amountMinor, String token, String email) {
        if (!inventory.reserve(sku)) throw new IllegalStateException("out of stock: " + sku);   // 1. reserve
        String receipt;
        try {
            receipt = payments.charge(amountMinor, token);                                     // 2. charge
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            inventory.release(sku);                                                            // 3. undo the reservation
            throw e;
        }
        notifier.send(email, "paid " + receipt);                                               // 4. tell the customer
        return receipt;
    }
}
Kotlin
class CheckoutFacade(
    private val inventory: Inventory,
    private val payments: Payments,
    private val notifier: Notifier,
) {
    fun checkout(sku: String, amountMinor: Long, token: String, email: String): String {
        check(inventory.reserve(sku)) { "out of stock: $sku" }                     // 1. reserve
        val receipt = try {
            payments.charge(amountMinor, token)                                     // 2. charge
        } catch (e: RuntimeException) {
            inventory.release(sku)                                                  // 3. undo the reservation
            throw e
        }
        notifier.send(email, "paid $receipt")                                       // 4. tell the customer
        return receipt
    }
}

The facade owns two decisions: the order of the steps, and what a failure at each step means. Charging before reserving would take money for stock you don't have. A declined card must release the reservation. Those rules now live in one tested place, and each caller is one line.

Nothing in either language replaces Facade; records and constructor injection only make it shorter. The risk is growth. A facade should orchestrate and nothing else: no amount maths, no vendor codes, no SQL. When it reaches forty methods, it has become the god service it was meant to hide, so split it by use case (CheckoutFacade, RefundFacade).

One Java gotcha showed up while compiling this example. A record component can't be called notify: javac reports "illegal record component name", because the accessor notify() would clash with Object.notify(). The same goes for wait, hashCode, toString, getClass and the other no-argument Object methods. A Kotlin property named notify compiles to getNotify() and is fine.

try.title: Break the facade's cleanup rule
steps: Run CheckoutFacadeDemo in either language and read the still reserved line.
Remove the try/catch around the charge, so a decline no longer releases the stock. Predict the still reserved line, then run.
Restore it. In the Java version only, rename the record component notifier to notify (and its use inside checkout). Compile.

code.title: CheckoutFacadeDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l04; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Set; /** A facade over inventory, payments and notifications: one call, the right order, cleanup on failure. */ public class CheckoutFacadeDemo { interface Inventory { boolean reserve(String sku); void release(String sku); } interface Payments { String charge(long amountMinor, String token); } interface Notifier { void send(String to, String message); } record CheckoutFacade(Inventory inventory, Payments payments, Notifier notifier) { String checkout(String sku, long amountMinor, String token, String email) { if (!inventory.reserve(sku)) throw new IllegalStateException("out of stock: " + sku); // 1. reserve String receipt; try { receipt = payments.charge(amountMinor, token); // 2. charge } catch (RuntimeException e) { inventory.release(sku); // 3. undo the reservation throw e; } notifier.send(email, "paid " + receipt); // 4. tell the customer return receipt; } } public static void main(String[] args) { Set<String> reserved = new HashSet<>(); Inventory inventory = new Inventory() { public boolean reserve(String sku) { return reserved.add(sku); } public void release(String sku) { reserved.remove(sku); } }; Payments payments = (amount, token) -> { if (token.equals("tok_declined")) throw new IllegalStateException("card declined"); return "R-" + amount; }; Notifier notifier = (to, message) -> System.out.println(" mail to " + to + ": " + message); CheckoutFacade facade = new CheckoutFacade(inventory, payments, notifier); System.out.println("receipt: " + facade.checkout("sku-1", 1_250, "tok_ok", "anna@example.com")); try { facade.checkout("sku-2", 990, "tok_declined", "anna@example.com"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("failed: " + e.getMessage() + "; still reserved: " + reserved); } } }

alt.title: CheckoutFacadeDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l04 // A facade over inventory, payments and notifications: one call, the right order, cleanup on failure. interface Inventory { fun reserve(sku: String): Boolean; fun release(sku: String) } fun interface Payments { fun charge(amountMinor: Long, token: String): String } fun interface Notifier { fun send(to: String, message: String) } class CheckoutFacade( private val inventory: Inventory, private val payments: Payments, private val notifier: Notifier, ) { fun checkout(sku: String, amountMinor: Long, token: String, email: String): String { check(inventory.reserve(sku)) { "out of stock: $sku" } // 1. reserve val receipt = try { payments.charge(amountMinor, token) // 2. charge } catch (e: RuntimeException) { inventory.release(sku) // 3. undo the reservation throw e } notifier.send(email, "paid $receipt") // 4. tell the customer return receipt } } fun main() { val reserved = mutableSetOf<String>() val inventory = object : Inventory { override fun reserve(sku: String) = reserved.add(sku) override fun release(sku: String) { reserved.remove(sku) } } val payments = Payments { amount, token -> check(token != "tok_declined") { "card declined" } "R-$amount" } val notifier = Notifier { to, message -> println(" mail to $to: $message") } val facade = CheckoutFacade(inventory, payments, notifier) println("receipt: " + facade.checkout("sku-1", 1_250, "tok_ok", "anna@example.com")) try { facade.checkout("sku-2", 990, "tok_declined", "anna@example.com") } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("failed: ${e.message}; still reserved: $reserved") } }

try.expect: The first run mails a receipt for sku-1, then prints failed: card declined; still reserved: [sku-1]: the declined order gave sku-2 back. Without the catch, the line ends [sku-1, sku-2], so a declined card holds stock until someone notices. The rename gives error: illegal record component name notify. The Kotlin class can have a property called notify.

sections.h: Ports and adapters: where the translation lives
sections.html:
Adapter and Facade both wrap something, and so do Decorator, Proxy and Bridge. Structure won't tell them apart. Intent will:

Pattern Wraps Offers Why
Adapter one object you can't change a different interface: yours make it fit your port
Facade several objects a new, simpler interface hide a sequence of calls
Decorator one object the same interface add behavior (Decorator and Proxy, lesson 5 of this track)
Proxy one object the same interface control access (lesson 5 of this track)
Bridge an implementation you pick your abstraction vary two dimensions (lesson 6 of this track)

In a service built with ports and adapters (often called hexagonal architecture), you see Adapter and Facade on one picture. The payment logic sits in the middle and talks only to ports: CardAuthorizer, Ledger, Notifier. Adapters sit on the edge, one per technology: the issuer SDK adapter, an Oracle ledger, a Kafka notifier. The facade is the front door, where a REST resource or a Kafka consumer makes one call.

That layout pays off twice. Switching issuers means writing one new adapter, and nothing in the middle changes. And the middle is tested with lambdas: new CheckoutFacade((pan, amount, currency) -> new Approved("A1"), ledger, notifier) needs no SDK, no database and no broker.

Domain-driven design calls a thick layer of adapters an anti-corruption layer: the place where the vendor's model (response code "51", numeric currency "978", amounts as strings) is translated into yours, so it never spreads. If you find "51" in a service class, the layer has a hole. The lab is that layer in miniature: an adapter that keeps an issuer SDK's quirks to itself, and a facade that callers can use without knowing the steps.

figure.caption: Callers make one call to the facade. Your code talks only to ports, and adapters on the edge translate to each vendor.

analogy: An adapter is the travel plug you carry abroad: the hotel's socket stays the same, your charger stays the same, and the plug translates between them. A facade is the hotel's front desk: you ask for a taxi to the airport at six, and the desk deals with the taxi company, the wake-up call and the bill. You never call the taxi company yourself. The analogy breaks on errors: a travel plug either fits or it doesn't, but a software adapter must also translate the vendor's failures into yours, and a leaky one passes the foreign voltage straight through.
world: Your Quarkus services already have ports and adapters, even if nobody calls them that: a REST client interface for a PSP, a @ApplicationScoped bean that wraps the issuer SDK, a Kafka emitter behind a Notifier. Check where the vendor's vocabulary ends. A response code "05" in a Temporal activity, or a vendor exception caught in a REST resource, means the adapter is leaking. Temporal makes this concrete: activity retry policies decide on exception types, so translate vendor errors into your own retryable and non-retryable exceptions inside the adapter, where you know which is which. And a checkout facade is a natural Temporal workflow later, once the steps need durable retries.
mistake: The most common mistake is the leaky adapter: it wraps the vendor's method calls but lets the vendor's model through. The adapter rethrows SdkException (or wraps it in a RuntimeException that callers unwrap), returns the vendor's response code as a string, or exposes the vendor's DTOs in its method signatures. It happens because translating every code and error feels like busywork when there is only one vendor. Then the second issuer arrives, and every service that checks "51" has to change. Translate everything at the boundary into your own sealed results and exceptions, and test the adapter against a fake of the vendor class.

compare.title: An anti-corruption adapter for a PSP webhook

java.title: PspWebhookAdapter.java
java.html: // the vendor's webhook body, with the vendor's names record PspWebhook(String type, String pspRef, String amtMinor, String ccy) {} // our model of what happened sealed interface PaymentEvent { record Captured(String paymentRef, long amountMinor, String currency) implements PaymentEvent {} record Refunded(String paymentRef, long amountMinor) implements PaymentEvent {} record Ignored(String why) implements PaymentEvent {} } final class PspWebhookAdapter { private PspWebhookAdapter() {} static PaymentEvent toEvent(PspWebhook w) { return switch (w.type()) { // vendor strings are an open set, so a default is right here case "charge.captured" -> new PaymentEvent.Captured(w.pspRef(), Long.parseLong(w.amtMinor()), w.ccy().toUpperCase()); case "charge.refunded" -> new PaymentEvent.Refunded(w.pspRef(), Long.parseLong(w.amtMinor())); default -> new PaymentEvent.Ignored("unhandled PSP event " + w.type()); }; } }

kotlin.title: PspWebhookAdapter.kt
kotlin.html: // the vendor's webhook body, with the vendor's names data class PspWebhook(val type: String, val pspRef: String, val amtMinor: String, val ccy: String) // our model of what happened sealed interface PaymentEvent { data class Captured(val paymentRef: String, val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String) : PaymentEvent data class Refunded(val paymentRef: String, val amountMinor: Long) : PaymentEvent data class Ignored(val why: String) : PaymentEvent } // the adapter as an extension: reads like a method on the vendor type fun PspWebhook.toEvent(): PaymentEvent = when (type) { // open set of vendor strings: else is right "charge.captured" -> PaymentEvent.Captured(pspRef, amtMinor.toLong(), ccy.uppercase()) "charge.refunded" -> PaymentEvent.Refunded(pspRef, amtMinor.toLong()) else -> PaymentEvent.Ignored("unhandled PSP event $type") }

compare.note: The translation is identical: vendor strings in, a sealed event of our own out. Kotlin writes it as an extension on the vendor type, so call sites read webhook.toEvent(); Java needs a static method on a holder class, so they read PspWebhookAdapter.toEvent(webhook). In bytecode they are the same static method. Both use a catch-all branch on purpose: vendor event types are an open set you don't control, unlike your own sealed types, where a missing case should break the build. Code that consumes PaymentEvent then switches over it with no default. Neither language makes Adapter unnecessary; Kotlin just makes the data-mapping kind cheaper to write.

worked.title: Wrap a vendor FX feed behind a port, then test without it

steps.say: A pricing service calls a vendor FX feed directly. The feed returns strings like "EURUSD=1.0842;ts=1730000000" and throws a checked FeedException. Before reading on, list every vendor detail that leaks into priceInUsd.
steps.code: class Pricer { private final RateFeedClient feed = new RateFeedClient("https://fx.vendor.example"); long priceInUsd(long amountMinorEur) throws FeedException { String raw = feed.quote("EURUSD"); // vendor pair format BigDecimal rate = new BigDecimal(raw.substring(raw.indexOf('=') + 1, raw.indexOf(';'))); return new BigDecimal(amountMinorEur).multiply(rate).setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).longValueExact(); } }

alt.html: class Pricer { private val feed = RateFeedClient("https://fx.vendor.example") fun priceInUsd(amountMinorEur: Long): Long { val raw = feed.quote("EURUSD") // vendor pair format; FeedException leaks unseen val rate = BigDecimal(raw.substringAfter('=').substringBefore(';')) return BigDecimal(amountMinorEur).multiply(rate).setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).longValueExact() } }

steps.say: Four leaks: the pair format, the response format, the checked exception, and the hard-wired URL. Define the port in your words first. It says nothing about strings or vendors, and an empty result means "no rate right now".
steps.code: interface FxRates { Optional<BigDecimal> rate(String from, String to); // 1. our words: currencies in, a rate or nothing out } class Pricer { private final FxRates rates; Pricer(FxRates rates) { this.rates = rates; } OptionalLong priceInUsd(long amountMinorEur) { return rates.rate("EUR", "USD") .map(r -> new BigDecimal(amountMinorEur).multiply(r).setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).longValueExact()) .map(OptionalLong::of).orElse(OptionalLong.empty()); } }

alt.html: fun interface FxRates { fun rate(from: String, to: String): BigDecimal? // 1. our words: currencies in, a rate or null out } class Pricer(private val rates: FxRates) { fun priceInUsd(amountMinorEur: Long): Long? = rates.rate("EUR", "USD")?.let { BigDecimal(amountMinorEur).multiply(it).setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).longValueExact() } }

steps.say: Now the adapter. Everything the vendor knows lives here: how pairs are spelled, how answers are packed, and which exception it throws. Why return empty instead of rethrowing on FeedException? Because the port promised "a rate or nothing", and the pricer decides what nothing means.
steps.code: final class VendorFxRates implements FxRates { private final RateFeedClient feed; VendorFxRates(RateFeedClient feed) { this.feed = feed; } public Optional<BigDecimal> rate(String from, String to) { try { String raw = feed.quote(from + to); // 2. our pair, their format return Optional.of(new BigDecimal(raw.substring(raw.indexOf('=') + 1, raw.indexOf(';')))); } catch (FeedException | RuntimeException e) { // 3. their failure, our answer return Optional.empty(); } } }

alt.html: class VendorFxRates(private val feed: RateFeedClient) : FxRates { override fun rate(from: String, to: String): BigDecimal? = try { val raw = feed.quote(from + to) // 2. our pair, their format BigDecimal(raw.substringAfter('=').substringBefore(';')) } catch (e: FeedException) { // 3. their failure, our answer null } catch (e: RuntimeException) { null } }

steps.say: Test the two halves separately. The pricer gets a lambda. The adapter gets a fake feed, a subclass of the vendor client that returns canned strings, which is how the lab tests its issuer adapter.
steps.code: // 4. the core, with no vendor at all assertThat(new Pricer((from, to) -> Optional.of(new BigDecimal("1.0842"))).priceInUsd(10_000)).hasValue(10_842); // 5. the adapter, against a fake of the vendor class RateFeedClient fake = new RateFeedClient("unused") { @Override public String quote(String pair) { return "EURUSD=1.0842;ts=1730000000"; } }; assertThat(new VendorFxRates(fake).rate("EUR", "USD")).contains(new BigDecimal("1.0842"));

alt.html: // 4. the core, with no vendor at all assertThat(Pricer { _, _ -> BigDecimal("1.0842") }.priceInUsd(10_000)).isEqualTo(10_842L) // 5. the adapter, against a fake of the vendor class (open in the SDK, or use an interface) val fake = object : RateFeedClient("unused") { override fun quote(pair: String) = "EURUSD=1.0842;ts=1730000000" } assertThat(VendorFxRates(fake).rate("EUR", "USD")).isEqualTo(BigDecimal("1.0842"))

lab.title: An issuer SDK adapter and a checkout facade
steps: Read LegacyIssuerSdk.java, CardAuthorizer.java and Amounts.java. They are given; don't edit them. Run the tests: all ten fail.

Write IssuerSdkAdapter.authorize. Call sdk.auth with Amounts.toDecimal and Amounts.numericCode, catch SdkException and return Unavailable(e.getMessage()), then split the response on | and map the code with a switch.

Write CheckoutFacade.checkout as a switch over the AuthResult. Approved: post, send the receipt (catching a failing notifier), return Paid. Declined: send the notice, return Declined. Unavailable: return RetryLater.
Run the tests until all ten pass.
hints: raw.split("\\|", -1) splits on a literal | and keeps the empty auth id in "51|". The pipe must be escaped, because split takes a regex.
A switch over the sealed AuthResult with case AuthResult.Approved ok -> ... needs no default: the compiler checks all three cases. In a switch expression, use yield to return from a block.
Wrap only the notifier call in try/catch. If the ledger post throws, let it propagate: an approved payment that isn't on the ledger is an incident, not something to swallow.

drill.title: An adapter from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A vendor GeoIpClient has String lookup(String ip) throws GeoException, returning text like "DE;Berlin". Your port is interface CountryOf { Optional<String> country(String ip); } (in Kotlin, fun interface CountryOf { fun country(ip: String): String? }). Write the adapter so the vendor's exception never escapes and an empty or malformed answer gives no country.

answer.html: final class GeoIpCountryOf implements CountryOf { private final GeoIpClient client; GeoIpCountryOf(GeoIpClient client) { this.client = client; } @Override public Optional<String> country(String ip) { try { String raw = client.lookup(ip); // their format: "DE;Berlin" if (raw == null) return Optional.empty(); String code = raw.split(";", 2)[0].trim(); return code.length() == 2 ? Optional.of(code) : Optional.empty(); } catch (GeoException e) { return Optional.empty(); // their failure stops here } } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class GeoIpCountryOf(private val client: GeoIpClient) : CountryOf { override fun country(ip: String): String? = try { client.lookup(ip) // their format: "DE;Berlin" ?.substringBefore(';') ?.trim() ?.takeIf { it.length == 2 } } catch (e: GeoException) { null // their failure stops here } }

recap: An adapter makes a class you can't change fit your port. It translates arguments on the way in, and results and errors on the way out.
Keep vendor types, codes and exceptions inside the adapter. A "51" or an SdkException in a service class is a leak.
Java's checked exceptions stop a vendor IOException from escaping a port that doesn't declare it; Kotlin compiles the same leak silently.
For a one-method port, a lambda or a fun interface is the adapter. For data mapping in Kotlin, an extension like VendorTxn.toReceipt() is the light adapter; in Java it's a static method.
A facade gives callers one call for a multi-step job and owns the order of the steps and what each failure means. Keep it orchestration only.
A Java record component can't be named notify, wait or another no-argument Object method.

explain.prompt: Explain to a new teammate why IssuerSdkAdapter returns Unavailable instead of letting SdkException through, and why CheckoutFacade swallows a failing receipt email but not a failing ledger post.
explain.answer: The adapter is the only class allowed to know the issuer's SDK. If SdkException escaped, every caller would import the vendor's type and decide on its status codes, and switching issuers would mean changing all of them. So the adapter turns it into our own result, Unavailable, and the facade turns that into RetryLater. In the facade, the order matters: once the card is approved, the money moved, so the ledger post must happen, and if it fails, that's an incident we must see, so it propagates. The receipt email is best effort. A broken mail server shouldn't turn a completed payment into an error the customer retries, which could charge them twice.

deeper.html:
The JDK has adapters you use daily. InputStreamReader adapts a byte stream into a character stream; its Javadoc calls it a bridge from byte streams to character streams, which shows how loosely the pattern names get used. Arrays.asList adapts an array into a fixed-size List that writes through to the array. Collections.enumeration and Enumeration.asIterator() (Java 9) adapt between the old and new iteration interfaces.

The GoF book describes two kinds of adapter. An object adapter holds the vendor object and delegates to it, as in this lesson. A class adapter inherits from the vendor class and implements your interface at the same time. Java and Kotlin allow the second only when the vendor class is open, and it is usually worse: your adapter inherits every public method of the SDK, so callers can bypass your translation. Prefer the object adapter.

Kotlin's by delegation (in Decorator and Proxy, lesson 5 of this track) can build an adapter that forwards most of an interface unchanged and overrides the few methods that need translation. That works when the two interfaces are almost the same, such as two versions of your own API. For a vendor SDK with a different model, write the translation out; it is the part that deserves a review.

Facades and transactions mix badly in one way. If a Spring or Quarkus facade method is @Transactional and calls an external issuer inside the transaction, a 120 ms issuer call holds a database connection for 120 ms. With a pool of 20 connections, a slow issuer starves the database. Charge first, outside the transaction, then post to the ledger in a short one, and make the post idempotent so a retry can't double-post.
